chapter_theme: The man's first sight of the woman, told as an injury: her beauty and returned gaze attack him like a goddess, an army, Death and a rutting elephant. The chapter treats love's beginning as the defeat of a strong man, and ends by claiming that love, unlike liquor, intoxicates through sight alone.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes follow what wounds him: her whole form (1081), her returned glance and eyes (1082-1086), her breasts (1087), her forehead (1088), her ornaments (1089). 1090 turns to reading her intent and opens the way to the next chapter.

1081.reading: The man, on first seeing her, cannot tell whether this woman in heavy earrings is a goddess, a rare peahen or a human being, and his heart reels.
1081.nuance: The three guesses aren't mere compliments. Parimelazhagar ties each to evidence: her indescribable form and his distress suggest a goddess, her grace and the grove suggest a peahen, and the way she looks back suggests a woman. Kalaignar's rendering drops the goddess and gives 'beauty that torments me' instead.

1082.reading: The man says that when she answers his look with her own, it is as if a goddess who strikes on her own had brought an army with her.
1082.nuance: The returned look is the blow. Parimelazhagar says he has now settled that she is human, so the goddess of 1081 survives only as a figure, and his pain has grown from her beauty to her meaningful glance.

1083.reading: The man says he never knew what Death was, and now he does: it has a woman's grace and large eyes that make war.
1083.nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses the first line as a contrast between hearsay and experience: Death was something known from what the learned say, and only now seen. He adds that the man calls her Death because the suffering outweighs the pleasure.

1084.reading: The man says the eyes of this artless, womanly girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them, and he sets those eyes against, or alongside, her gentleness.

positions.position: அமர்த்தன means the eyes are at odds with her gentle nature; they are cruel where she is not.
The word means the eyes fit her: they suit the girl in the work they do.
The eyes are a puzzling contradiction in someone so womanly.

1085.reading: The man asks whether it is Death, an eye or a doe, since the young woman's look has the nature of all three.
1085.nuance: The list holds opposites: the look kills, it seeks him out, and it startles like a frightened animal. Parimelazhagar sums this up as pleasure and pain given together, which sets up the double look of 1091.

1086.reading: The man says that if her curved brows would only stop bending and screen her eyes, those eyes could not cause him this trembling pain.
1086.nuance: The conceit turns on the word கோடா, 'unbending'. Parimelazhagar treats the brows as the eyes' close friends, who could restrain them only if they were straight themselves, because anyone who rebukes a friend must be upright. Manakkudavar reads a small scene into it: she has lowered her head and her brows now shade her eyes.

1087.reading: The man says the cloth over her firm breasts is like the face-cloth over the eyes of a rutting elephant.
1087.nuance: A covering usually suggests safety, but this one announces danger. Parimelazhagar makes modesty the reason for the cloth, while the man, seeing strength through it, thinks of what it holds back. Manakkudavar has the man address her directly as மாதரே, while Parimelazhagar has him speak about her.

1088.reading: The man laments that his might, feared in battle even by enemies who never met him there, has broken before her bright forehead alone.
1088.nuance: The ஓ marks wonder at the mismatch: so great a strength and so small a thing as a forehead. Parimelazhagar is careful to note that this isn't boasting, because the man is grieving for what he has lost.

1089.reading: The man asks what use foreign ornaments are to one who already has a doe's shy look and modesty.
1089.nuance: It sounds like a pure compliment, but both older commentators hear a complaint. For Parimelazhagar, whoever adorned her lacks sense, because the jewels burden her and harm him; for Manakkudavar, he praises her while seeming to accuse her of cruelty.

1090.reading: Brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, not those who merely see it as love does; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1090.nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies an unspoken close: love is better than liquor, yet he hasn't obtained it because he hasn't yet read her intent. He also takes காமம் here to mean the person in whom love is enjoyed.

positions.position: The man speaks as he sets out to read her intent.
The woman thinks this, pained after seeing the man, which reverses the chapter's point of view.

links.note: The warrior of 774 pulls a spear from his own body and laughs. The warrior of 1088 has that same reputation and is broken by a forehead. The Kural's courage has no defence against this enemy.

1014 calls modesty the ornament of the great, and without it their proud bearing is a disease. 1089 uses the same idea for a girl's beauty, so the ethical chapter's metaphor returns as a lover's literal claim that jewels are redundant.

Both set love above liquor for delighting through sight. 1090 says it at the first encounter and 1281 says it deep in the relationship, so the comparison holds from the start of love through its maturity.

source_issues: 1083: Parimelazhagar's text has பண்தகையுடனே where பெண்தகையுடனே seems intended, and his gloss has பெண் தகையாள் where the verse has பெண்டகையால்.
